items.title: Submask Enumeration Battery
items.statement: Given n≤20 masks, compute Σ over pairs (a,b) where a|b==FULL of value[a]&value[b] using submask walks within complexity budget.

solutionCode.label: descending submask walk, with the 3^n accounting
solutionCode.py:
def all_submasks(m: int) -> list:
    """SUBMASK IDIOM: sub = (sub - 1) & m steps to the next smaller submask.
    Starting at m and stopping after 0 enumerates every submask exactly once."""
    out = []
    sub = m
    while True:
        out.append(sub)
        if sub == 0:
            break                    # test AFTER appending, or 0 is skipped
        sub = (sub - 1) & m
    return out


def pair_sum(value: list, n: int) -> int:
    """Sum over pairs (a, b) with a | b == FULL of value[a] & value[b].

    3^n ACCOUNTING: a mask with k set bits has 2^k submasks, and C(n,k) masks
    have k bits, so total work is sum_k C(n,k) * 2^k = (1+2)^n = 3^n."""
    full = (1 << n) - 1
    total = 0
    for a in range(full + 1):
        need = full ^ a              # b must contain at least these bits
        free = a                     # b may also contain any submask of a
        sub = free
        while True:
            total += value[a] & value[need | sub]
            if sub == 0:
                break
            sub = (sub - 1) & free
    return total

items.complexity: Total 3^n, not 4^n. Each mask m walks its 2^popcount(m) submasks, and summing that over all masks gives 3^n by the binomial identity.

followups.q: Why does (sub - 1) & m step to the next submask?
followups.a: Subtracting 1 borrows through the trailing zeros of sub, producing a pattern that is numerically just below it. ANDing with m discards any bits that are not in m, landing on the largest submask of m strictly smaller than sub. Iterating gives every submask in descending order, each exactly once.

followups.q: Why must the zero test come after the body?
followups.a: The loop condition would exit before processing sub = 0, silently dropping the empty submask — which is a legitimate one. Testing at the bottom processes 0 and then breaks. It is the classic do-while shape, and forgetting it costs exactly one missing case per mask.

items.title: Subarray Xor = K Counter
items.statement: Section engine verbatim; extend to count with at most k flips variant aloud.

solutionCode.label: prefix XOR with a frequency map — same skeleton as prefix sums
solutionCode.py:
def count_subarrays_with_xor(a: list, k: int) -> int:
    freq = {0: 1}             # the empty prefix, so whole-array matches count
    prefix = total = 0
    for x in a:
        prefix ^= x
        # want prefix ^ earlier == k, i.e. earlier == prefix ^ k
        total += freq.get(prefix ^ k, 0)
        freq[prefix] = freq.get(prefix, 0) + 1    # insert AFTER probing
    return total
# WHY XOR REPLACES SUBTRACTION: with sums, subarray = prefix[r] - prefix[l-1],
# so you look up prefix - k. XOR is its own inverse, so you look up prefix ^ k.
# Same prefix technique, different group operation.

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n). Identical shape to LC560 subarray-sum-equals-k, with XOR replacing addition.

followups.q: Why does the map store counts rather than positions?
followups.a: The same prefix XOR can occur at many indices, and every one of them starts a valid subarray ending here. You need how many, not where. Storing a position keeps only the last and undercounts — exactly the same bug as in the prefix-sum version.

The empty prefix before index 0. Without it, a subarray starting at index 0 whose XOR equals k is never counted, because no earlier prefix of the right value has been recorded. It is the seed that makes whole-array and prefix-anchored matches work.

items.title: Single Number III (two loners)
items.statement: Two distinct odd-count elements; partition by lowest differing bit then XOR groups.

solutionCode.label: XOR everything, isolate a differing bit, split into two buckets

items.complexity: Time O(n) in two passes, space O(1).

followups.a: The problem states the two loners are distinct, and every other element appears twice and cancels. So mix equals p ^ q with p != q, which is non-zero by definition of XOR — two different values must differ in at least one bit. If they could be equal, the whole partition strategy would have nothing to split on.

followups.q: Does the choice of differing bit matter?
followups.a: No — any set bit of mix separates p from q, because that is what "set in p^q" means. The lowest is chosen only because mix & -mix isolates it in one operation. Picking the highest or any other set bit gives the same two answers, possibly in the other order.

items.title: Count Pairs With AND == 0 (SOS-lite)
items.statement: n≤10⁶ values <2²⁰. Full SOS table OR per-element submask complement walk — implement faster one after measuring.
hints: Naive complement-walk dies when many dense masks.

solutionCode.label: Sum over Subsets DP beats the naive complement walk on dense input
solutionCode.py:
def count_pairs_and_zero(values: list, B: int) -> int:
    """Count ordered pairs (i, j) with value[i] & value[j] == 0.

    A partner of x must be a SUBMASK of ~x, so the per-element answer is
    'how many values are submasks of ~x' -- what SOS DP tabulates."""
    size = 1 << B
    dp = [0] * size
    for v in values:
        dp[v] += 1                        # dp[m] starts as the exact count

    # SOS: after bit b's pass, dp[m] counts values that are submasks of m
    # considering only bits 0..b. B passes over 2^B entries.
    for b in range(B):
        bit = 1 << b
        for m in range(size):
            if m & bit:
                dp[m] += dp[m ^ bit]

    full = size - 1
    return sum(dp[full ^ v] for v in values)   # partners are submasks of ~v
# WHY NOT THE NAIVE WALK: enumerating every submask of ~v costs 2^popcount(~v).
# For SPARSE values, ~v is dense and that is up to 2^19 per element. SOS is a
# flat B * 2^B regardless of density.

items.complexity: SOS DP: O(B * 2^B) for B bits — about 20 * 10^6 = 2*10^7 for B = 20. The per-element submask walk is O(n * 2^popcount), which degenerates on dense masks.

followups.q: What exactly does dp[m] hold after the SOS passes?
followups.a: The number of input values that are submasks of m — that is, values v with v & m == v. Each bit pass merges in the counts from masks that differ only by that bit, so after all B passes every subset relationship has been accumulated. It is a subset-lattice prefix sum.

followups.q: When does the naive submask walk actually win?
followups.a: When the values are DENSE — many bits set — because then ~v is sparse and 2^popcount(~v) is small. Measure before choosing: the two approaches have opposite worst cases, and the problem statement rarely tells you which regime the data is in.

items.title: Bitwise ORs of All Subarrays
items.statement: Count DISTINCT or-values; rolling frontier set keeps ≤~21 entries per end (bits saturate).
hints: cur = cur | x applied to every prior OR; store new set only.

solutionCode.label: rolling frontier: ORs saturate, so only ~30 survive per end index

items.complexity: Time O(n * B) where B is about 30 — the frontier set can never exceed the bit width. Space O(n * B) for the global distinct set.

followups.q: Prove the frontier is bounded by the bit width.
followups.a: Fix the right end i and extend the left end outward. Each extension ORs in more elements, so the value is monotonically non-decreasing in its set bits — it can only gain bits, never lose them. A value with B bits can gain a bit at most B times, so at most B+1 distinct values ever appear. For 32-bit inputs that is 31 or so.

followups.q: Why does the naive O(n^2) approach fail here?
followups.a: With n = 5*10^4 the number of subarrays is 1.25*10^9 — too many to enumerate even though each OR is O(1). The frontier trick exploits the saturation property to collapse those n subarrays per end index into ~30 distinct values, which is the whole algorithm.

items.title: Overflow-Free Average & Max Library
items.statement: Implement avg/max/min/abs helpers; fuzz against naive versions on adversarial extremes incl. INT_MIN.

solutionCode.label: overflow-free helpers, with every UB guard documented inline

items.complexity: All O(1). The point is correctness at the extremes, not speed.

followups.q: Why does (a & b) + ((a ^ b) >> 1) equal the average?
followups.a: Split each bit position into "both set" and "exactly one set". Both-set positions contribute their full value to each operand, so they contribute once to the average — that is a & b. Exactly-one positions contribute half — that is (a ^ b) >> 1. The sum is never formed, so it cannot overflow.

followups.q: Why is branchless abs undefined for INT_MIN?
followups.a: INT_MIN is -2147483648 but INT_MAX is only 2147483647, so +2147483648 has no 32-bit signed representation. The bit trick returns INT_MIN unchanged — a negative "absolute value". This is not a flaw in the trick; std::abs has the same undefined behaviour. Widening to 64 bits is the only correct fix.
